content: Retroviral intervention has the potential to alter or inhibit viral replication. In a primate model of simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) infection, dendritic-like cells at the site of inoculation were infected within the first 24 hours following mucosal exposure to a cell-free virus. Over the next 24 to 48 hours, these infected cells migrated to regional lymph nodes, and the virus became detectable in peripheral blood within five days. Theoretically, initiating antiretroviral post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) shortly after exposure could prevent or inhibit systemic infection by limiting viral proliferation in the initial target cells or lymph nodes. Efficacy of Antiretrovirals for PEP in Animal Studies Data from animal studies have been challenging to interpret due to difficulties in identifying an animal model that closely resembles human infection. Factors such as the choice of viral strain, inoculum size, route of inoculation, timing of prophylaxis initiation, and drug regimen have complicated the extrapolation of results to humans. However, recent methodological advancements have enabled more relevant studies. For instance, viral inocula used in animal studies have been reduced to levels more analogous to human exposures while still being sufficient to cause infection in control animals. These studies have provided promising evidence of the efficacy of post-exposure chemoprophylaxis. Studies in primates, as well as murine and feline models, have demonstrated that larger viral inocula reduce the efficacy of prophylaxis. Additionally, delaying the initiation of PEP, shortening its duration, or reducing the antiretroviral dose—either individually or in combination—has been shown to decrease prophylactic efficacy. For example, when (R)-9-(2-phosphonylmethoxypropyl) adenine (tenofovir) was administered 48 hours before, 4 hours after, or 24 hours after intravenous SIV inoculation in long-tailed macaques, a 4-week regimen prevented infection in all treated animals. A subsequent study confirmed the efficacy of tenofovir PEP when administered 24 hours after intravenous inoculation of an SIV dose that uniformly caused infection in untreated macaques. However, protection was incomplete if tenofovir administration was delayed to 48 or 72 hours post-exposure or if the total duration of treatment was shortened to 3 or 10 days. Efficacy of Antiretrovirals for PEP in Human Studies Limited data exist to assess the efficacy of PEP in humans. Seroconversion following occupational exposure to HIV-infected blood is infrequent, meaning that thousands of exposed healthcare personnel (HCP) would need to be enrolled in a prospective trial to achieve the statistical power necessary to directly demonstrate PEP efficacy. In a retrospective case-control study of HCP, after controlling for other risk factors for HIV transmission, the use of zidovudine (ZDV) as PEP was associated with an approximately 81% reduction in the risk of HIV infection (95% CI = 43%-94%). While these results suggest PEP efficacy, the study's limitations include the small number of cases studied and the use of cases and controls from different cohorts. In a multicenter trial, ZDV administered to HIV-infected pregnant women and their infants during pregnancy, labor, delivery, and postpartum reduced transmission by 67%. Notably, only part of the protective effect of ZDV was explained by the reduction of maternal HIV viral load, suggesting that ZDV prophylaxis involves mechanisms beyond reducing maternal viral burden. Since 1998, studies have emphasized the importance of PEP in preventing perinatal HIV transmission. In Africa, the combination of ZDV and lamivudine (3TC) reduced perinatal HIV transmission by 50% when administered during pregnancy, labor, and for one week postpartum, and by 37% when started at the onset of labor and continued for one week postpartum. Studies in the United States and Uganda have also demonstrated reduced rates of perinatal HIV transmission with abbreviated PEP regimens initiated intrapartum or within the first 48-72 hours of life. Limitations of Animal and Human Studies The limitations of both animal and human studies must be considered when reviewing evidence of PEP efficacy. The extent to which data from animal studies can be extrapolated to humans remains largely unknown. Additionally, the exposure route for mother-to-infant HIV transmission differs from occupational exposures, meaning these findings may not be directly applicable to PEP in HCP. Reports of PEP Failure There have been at least 21 reported cases of PEP failure to prevent HIV infection in HCP. In 16 of these cases, ZDV was used alone as a single agent; in two cases, ZDV and didanosine (ddI) were used in combination; and in three cases, more than three drugs were used for PEP. Thirteen of the source individuals were known to have been treated with antiretroviral therapy prior to the exposure. Antiretroviral resistance testing of the virus from the source individual was performed in seven instances, and in four cases, the transmitted HIV infection was found to have decreased sensitivity to ZDV and/or other drugs used for PEP.
